firm.summary: Fulton Asset Management (FAM) is a Chicago family office and investment platform. It buys and builds lower-middle-market industrial businesses with permanent family capital: no fund structure and no planned exit (fultonasset.com). FAM is the investment arm of the family behind The Imperial Group, a vertically integrated Chicago metals recycling, alloying and manufacturing group founded in 1962. Imperial is headquartered at 1700 W Fulton St, which likely explains the 'Fulton' name (inference). The Aug 2025 AFCO release says FAM owns and operates 'over 20 operations', including Imperial Group, Mayco Industries, Stainless Foundry & Engineering, Metaltec Steel Abrasives, Setna iO, Panther Metalflow, Transend Logistics and AFCO Industries. FAM rarely invests alone. Its recurring co-sponsors are Ashland Capital Partners (Chicago; owns nine lower-middle-market industrial businesses) and Lorentzen Investments, with Atlas Capital Ventures listed on Mayco. The identified portfolio clusters in non-ferrous and ferrous scrap recycling (copper and aluminum wire and cable), zinc, aluminum and lead alloys and mill products, castings, steel abrasives, CNC machining and fabrication, aviation aftermarket, and 3PL trucking. None of the identified holdings makes electrical equipment or transformers.
firm.history: 1962: Fred Weiss starts the family's industrial scrap and recycling business near West Fulton St and North Paulina St, Chicago [P: imperialgp.com/about-us; S: Recycling Today/PRWeb]. 1995: the group buys Imperial Zinc Corp. (zinc anodes and alloys), and the family's companies become known as the 'Imperial Zinc group' [W: TheOrg, Lusha]. c.2009 (est. from article age): Imperial Zinc/Imperial Aluminum buys a bankrupt secondary aluminum plant in Scottsboro, AL for $1.3M, together with a smelter in Minerva, OH. Scottsboro was later sold to Metal Source and Minerva was kept [S]. 2012: Midwest Industrial Metals (Northlake, IL) joins the group [S]. Date not confirmed (est. c.2012-13): investors including 'the principal owners of Imperial Zinc Corp., Chicago' buy Metalico's lead fabricating business, including Mayco Industries, for $31.3M [S: recyclingtoday.com]. 2014: Exeon Processors (Jonesboro, IN) is bought jointly by its management and the owners of the Imperial Zinc group [P: exeoninc.com/history]. Aug 2022: Metaltec. Feb 2024: Stainless Foundry & Engineering. Dec 2024: Imperial Group joins the Vinyl Sustainability Council. Jan 2025: Jason Kozin becomes CEO of FAM, which directories date as 'founded 2025'. Jul/Aug 2025: AFCO Industries. 2026: Setna iO buys a majority of J&C Aero, and FAM forms a strategic partnership with ZYCI CNC.
leadership: Jason S. Kozin: CEO of Fulton Asset Management since Jan 2025 (LinkedIn; quoted as CEO in the Business Wire release of Aug 25, 2025). Has held roles at The Imperial Group LLC since 2010 and is listed as a Partner of Imperial Group. Co-founded Setna iO (founded 2016). Spoke at Smart Business Dealmakers Chicago.
Zachary (Zach) Spellman: President, The Imperial Group (PRWeb, Dec 16, 2024).
Fred Weiss: founder of the original 1962 venture (imperialgp.com/about-us). Exact family relationship to Kozin not found.
Portfolio CEOs: Don Fowler (AFCO Industries, per KALB); Mat Staudinger (Stainless Foundry & Engineering CEO since Aug 7, 2025); Mitch Free and Shirene Free (ZYCI co-founders).

Co-sponsors and lenders: Ashland Capital Partners, Lorentzen Investments, Atlas Capital Ventures (on Mayco); CIBC (AFCO debt), Graycliff Partners and Fifth Third (Metaltec), GuardHill (SFE refinancing).
firm.investment_criteria: Sectors: metals, manufacturing and industrial services, per FAM's own site (fultonasset.com). A directory (privateequityinfo.com) adds aerospace, manufacturing, infrastructure and defense, plus precision machining, casting and forging, building products and real estate. Axial lists FAM as a Chicago family office (axial.net/company/fulton-asset-management). Size: no published revenue or EBITDA thresholds were found. Deal evidence: Panther Metalflow has about 40 employees and about $5.4M revenue (W, BuzzFile); ZYCI has 22-31 employees (W); FAM SFE Holdings LLC raised $6.0M of equity (Form D, Mar 12, 2024, formds.com); AFCO has 373 ESOP participants, with $65.5M paid to the 231 Central Louisiana participants alone (KALB). Estimate: FAM's target range is roughly $5M-150M revenue, or about $1M-20M EBITDA, based on observed targets and Axial's platform norm of $5-250M revenue and $0.5-25M EBITDA. Control: usually shared control with co-sponsors (Metaltec, SFE, AFCO), with management or founders often keeping equity. ZYCI is a minority or non-control 'strategic partnership' in which the founders remain significant owners (inference). Geography: US Midwest and South (IL, WI, MI, IN, OH, AL, LA, MS, GA), plus Setna iO's global network. Holding period: indefinite; the site states permanent capital, no fund structure and no planned exit.
firm.style: Family-office 'buy and build' with permanent capital and an operator background. (1) It is led by the operating family of a metals recycler and alloy producer, so the companies it buys tend to sit next to Imperial's metal flows: scrap steel feeds Metaltec's shot and grit; zinc die casting at Panther Metalflow sits beside Imperial Zinc; lead rolling at Mayco; copper and aluminum wire recovery at Exeon and Midwest Industrial Metals. (2) It co-sponsors with Chicago family offices (Ashland, Lorentzen) and finances with senior bank debt plus mezzanine (CIBC, Fifth Third, Graycliff). (3) It buys succession and liquidity situations: AFCO's ESOP repurchase strain, SFE's long-time owner exiting, and Metaltec's PE fund forced to divest. (4) Incumbent management usually stays. (5) Add-ons and international expansion happen inside holdings, as with Setna iO buying a majority of J&C Aero in 2026. (6) Smaller stakes, such as ZYCI, add capital for equipment, people and capacity. (7) It holds indefinitely with no exit horizon. Integration looks light: companies are run as separate units with no evidence of merging them into one operation.

portfolio.company: The Imperial Group (Imperial Recycling and group HQ)
portfolio.what_it_does: Family-owned, vertically integrated metals group founded 1962. It recovers scrap, processes and alloys metal, and manufactures, trades and moves it. Imperial Recycling specializes in recovering copper and aluminum from insulated wire, armored cable and oilfield cable, and is growing a PVC cable-jacket recycling operation (Vinyl Sustainability Council member since Dec 2024).
portfolio.capabilities: Non-ferrous scrap buying and processing; wire chopping and granulation; copper and aluminum recovery; PVC recovery; metals trading; logistics.
portfolio.locations: HQ 1700 W Fulton St, Chicago, IL (imperialgp.com). A third-party profile lists 1031 E 103rd St, Chicago.
portfolio.size_hint: Group revenue not disclosed; aggregator figures conflict. Est. likely $100M+ across all units (basis: four or more metal-producing and recycling plants and secondary smelters; an assumption, not found).
portfolio.acquired: Family-founded 1962 (the core family business, not an acquisition)
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Strong upstream and downstream link to grid metals. (a) It buys and processes copper and aluminum from insulated and armored utility and industrial cable. It could take utility scrap from reconductoring, end-of-life distribution transformers (copper and aluminum windings, steel tanks and cores) and substation teardowns. (b) It supplies secondary copper and aluminum units into the copper rod and aluminum alloy chain that feeds winding-wire and strip producers, indirectly. (c) Recycling copper and aluminum is a hedge against the copper spike that is squeezing transformer gross margins (+45% copper noted in the deep dive). (d) It could offer a closed-loop scrap buyback to transformer makers and rebuilders.

portfolio.what_it_does: Producer of zinc alloys and zinc anodes for construction, automotive and die-casting customers.
portfolio.capabilities: Zinc alloying; zinc anode production (cathodic protection, galvanizing and plating anodes); die-cast alloys.
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Moderate. Zinc is the main input to hot-dip galvanizing of transmission towers, substation steel structures and some pad-mount and pole hardware. Zinc anodes give cathodic protection to buried steel such as substation grounding, pipe-type cable and tanks. It could supply galvanizers serving the grid build-out. It does not sell to transformer makers directly.

portfolio.company: Imperial Aluminum (incl. Imperial Aluminum-Minerva LLC) and Imperial Alloys
portfolio.what_it_does: Secondary aluminum smelting. It converts recovered aluminum scrap into specification-grade alloys for die-casting and foundry customers. Imperial Alloys is a sister alloy unit whose details were not found.
portfolio.capabilities: Secondary aluminum smelting and alloying (ingot, possibly molten metal).
portfolio.locations: Minerva, OH smelter, still owned. A former Scottsboro, AL plant was bought out of bankruptcy and later sold to Metal Source.
portfolio.acquired: c.2009 (est.; Scottsboro plant plus Minerva smelter bought for $1.3M; article about 17 years old)
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Weak to moderate. Secondary die-cast and foundry alloys can go into cast transformer and switchgear hardware such as bushing caps, terminal connectors, radiator fittings and enclosure castings. Winding strip and foil needs EC-grade (1350) aluminum, which secondary smelters do not normally make. Could absorb aluminum winding scrap from distribution transformer recycling.

portfolio.what_it_does: Non-ferrous scrap processor: insulated wire, copper, aluminum, brass.
portfolio.capabilities: Scrap buying, sorting and wire processing
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Moderate to strong. A collection point for copper, aluminum and brass scrap from utilities, electrical contractors, transformer rebuilders and data-center construction offcuts in the Chicago area. Could take end-of-life transformer windings and bushings.

portfolio.what_it_does: Wire and cable processor: granulates insulated copper and aluminum wire into clean metal chops.
portfolio.capabilities: Wire chopping and granulation. It expanded capacity with an SBA 504 loan (First Merchants Bank / Indiana Statewide CDC).
portfolio.acquired: 2014 (bought jointly by management and the owners of the Imperial Zinc group)
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Strong for copper recovery. It processes utility and industrial cable scrap into copper and aluminum chops that go back to rod mills, the start of the winding-wire chain. It benefits directly from reconductoring, undergrounding and replacement volumes in the grid build-out.

portfolio.what_it_does: Calls itself the largest, most diversified US maker of non-battery lead products, and runs what Livingstone calls 'the nation's largest lead rolling mill'. Products: sheet lead, lead brick, radiation shielding, ballast weights, roofing and plumbing lead, flashings, lead shot, anodes, solder, pipe.
portfolio.capabilities: Lead alloy rolling mill; casting; extrusion; shot tower; fabrication
portfolio.locations: Birmingham, AL (18 W Oxmoor Rd, rolling mill); shot tower in Granite City, IL. Metalico's former lead businesses also included California.
portfolio.size_hint: $35.8M revenue (W, Kona Equity aggregator); bought from Metalico for $31.3M (Recycling Today)
portfolio.acquired: Date not confirmed (est. c.2012-13). Bought from Metalico by investors including the principal owners of Imperial Zinc; now jointly owned by Imperial Group, Lorentzen and Ashland (Atlas Capital Ventures also listed on PitchBook).
portfolio.transformer_chain_link: Limited. Lead has no direct transformer use. Small niches: lead sheathing alloys for HV underground and submarine cable; radiation shielding for nuclear and medical sites; vibration-damping or ballast pads for heavy equipment. Lead-acid battery recycling (substation DC and data-center UPS) is outside Mayco's non-battery focus.

Already serves power generation and nuclear OEMs. Possible castings for transformer and grid equipment: stainless and bronze-alternative valve bodies (drain and sampling valves), pump housings for oil coolers, cooler and radiator flanges, bushing and tap-changer hardware, and corrosion-resistant substation hardware. Could also cast for gas-turbine and generator OEMs serving data-center power.

portfolio.size_hint: Not found. Est. $20-50M revenue (basis: one of three leading US steel abrasive makers, single plant; assumption).

fulton_research.notes:
FAM sits in the transformer and grid supply chain mainly as a metals recycler and supplier, not as a likely transformer maker or acquirer. The overlaps:
- **Copper and aluminum wire/cable recycling** (Imperial Recycling, Midwest Industrial Metals, Exeon): a hedge against the copper-cost problem flagged in the deep dive, and a possible closed-loop scrap partner for transformer makers and rebuilders.
- **Zinc** (Imperial Zinc): feeds galvanizing of grid steel.
- **Steel shot and grit** (Metaltec): a direct consumable for transformer tank and enclosure blast lines.
- **Stainless and high-alloy castings** (SFE): already sells to power-generation and nuclear customers.
- **Fabrication and CNC** (AFCO, Panther, ZYCI): could make enclosure and hardware sub-assemblies.
- **Flatbed and cross-border freight** (Transend): fits distribution-class units moving from Mexico.

**FAM as a partner for the deep dive's 'buy or partner into a plant' route:**
- None of the 13 identified holdings makes transformers, switchgear or electrical steel, and none has a test bay or utility qualification.
- FAM's buyer profile does fit a 10-60 MVA brownfield entry: permanent capital, co-sponsored lower-middle-market control deals, succession and ESOP situations, metals-heavy Midwest and South footprint.
- Ashland's precast holdings would add more (see co-sponsor holdings below).

**Gaps and caveats:**
1. The fultonasset.com portfolio page and the Axial criteria could not be read directly. WebFetch is blocked, and the Axial snippet showed no revenue or EBITDA figures, so all size criteria above are estimates.
2. Only about 13 of the 'over 20 operations' were identified. The rest are probably other Imperial Group units and real estate entities.
3. The Mayco purchase year is unconfirmed (est. c.2012-13).
4. The Imperial Zinc purchase year (1995) comes only from directories.
5. The Panther Metalflow and ZYCI dates are inferred from an LEI creation date and LinkedIn post ages.
6. All revenue figures for Mayco, Panther and Transend come from aggregators (W).
7. The family link between Kozin and founder Fred Weiss was not established.
8. A Smart Business Dealmakers Chicago 2025 honoree page appeared in results but Kozin's honor was not confirmed.

**Ashland co-sponsor holdings (not confirmed as FAM-owned):** Boccella Precast, NAPCO Precast, Dedoes Industries, GMI Group (PVF), NewFound Rentals, and KBK Industries (storage tanks, exited Jan 2026).
- NAPCO and Boccella make precast concrete. Precast transformer pads, vaults and substation trench are a real grid link if FAM co-invests there; verify.
- Lorentzen Investments' wider holdings were not researched.

chain_research.notes:
US market size: analyst figures disagree by 2-4x, mostly because their scopes differ.
- Mordor: US transformer market $7.90B in 2025, power transformers 56.7% (~$4.5B, computed); US distribution $3.41B (2025), $5.60B by 2031.
- MarketsandMarkets: US distribution $4.30B (2025), $6.01B by 2030.
- Expert Market Research: US distribution $11.84B (2025).
- Arizton: all US transformers $16.5B (2024), $24.85B by 2030.
- Wood Mackenzie publishes no total. It puts 2026 deficits at 15% for power transformers and 8% for substation units, and US data-center electrical equipment (all types) at $20B rising to $65B by 2030.

Bottom-up from this slice (midpoints of builder estimates, North America, 2025-26 run-rate, including Mexican/Canadian domestic sales and aftermarket):
- Large power/EHV: ~$7.5-8B, including ~$1.2B of imports not attributed to a named builder.
- Medium power/substation: ~$3.8B, mostly Prolec.
- Distribution/pad-mount: ~$6.3B, including ~$1.5B of imports.
- Dry-type: ~$2B.
- Aftermarket: ~$0.85B.
- Solid-state: <$0.05B.
- Total: ~$20B. That is above Arizton's 2024 figure, which fits 2025-26 price growth (transformer PPI +7.6-8.7% YoY) and the wider scope. Treat it as order-of-magnitude.

Concentration: Prolec GE (~$3-3.6B) is the largest. Eaton, HD Hyundai, Hitachi, Howard, VTC and Hyosung are each ~$1-1.6B. Together these seven hold roughly half of North American supply (computed from midpoints).

Disclosed vs estimated: only Forgent ($1.42B FY26), Hammond (C$324.8M in Q2 2026), Prolec (~$3B 2025E, ~$900M in Q2 2026), HD Hyundai North America (KRW 541.9B in Q2 2026), Hyosung's US subsidiaries (KRW 1.49T in 2025) and JST USA (RMB 1.307B in H1 2026) disclose figures. The HD Hyundai and Hyosung figures include reactors and switchgear. All private-company revenues are estimates from aggregators or headcount times revenue per employee: VTC, Howard, ERMCO, Central Moloney, Delta Star, Sunbelt Solomon, Giga and PTT/Niagara.

Assumed FX: 1,400 KRW, 7.2 RMB and 1.37 CAD per USD. Forgent's transformer share of revenue is not disclosed; I assumed 35-55%.

Edge values split each builder's estimated revenue across customer types by assumption. Named relationships in the edge bases:
- AEP's approved 500-765 kV vendor list (Hitachi).
- AEP-Quanta EHV development agreement (PTT).
- HD Hyundai's $721M Big Tech framework through 2028, plus its 765 kV utility orders.
- Hyosung's $287M of tech-company orders and a KRW ~787B 765 kV contract (year unconfirmed).
- WAPA LPT blanket purchase agreement (VTC).
- Municipal bids: JEA (WEG, VanTran, Central Moloney), Lafayette (Eaglerise), Austin Energy (Kerec, Sungjin, Taihan), Zeeland (ERMCO, GE units) and Coldwater (Sunbelt Solomon).
- RWE Americas pilot (Heron Power).

Ownership watch: Delta Star (going to MacLean) and Sunbelt Solomon (going to TJC) are pending sales. JST and Eaglerise are Chinese-owned and exposed to DOE's EO 14421 rules (due ~late Dec 2026).

nodes.name: Cleveland-Cliffs Mining & Pelletizing
nodes.description: Cliffs' captive iron ore mines and pellet plants in Minnesota and Michigan. They reach GOES only indirectly, through DR-grade pellets for the Toledo HBI plant.

nodes.name: Cleveland-Cliffs Toledo HBI plant
nodes.description: Hot-briquetted iron plant at the Port of Toledo, built to feed Great Lakes EAFs. Assumed (not verified) to supply part of the metallic charge for Butler Works' EAF melt shop.

nodes.name: US ferrous scrap and pig iron suppliers (incl. Cliffs' FPT)
nodes.description: Scrap processors and pig iron importers that supply the low-residual metallics an EAF needs for electrical steel. Cliffs owns scrap processor Ferrous Processing & Trading (acquired 2021, from background knowledge).
nodes.ownership: Mixed (Cliffs-owned FPT plus independents and importers)

nodes.name: Ferroglobe
nodes.description: Largest US producer of ferrosilicon and silicon metal, with US smelters (e.g., Beverly OH; Calvert City KY via CC Metals & Alloys, from background knowledge). GOES carries ~3% silicon, added as ferrosilicon.
nodes.size_label: 2025 shipments: FeSi 151,876 t; silicon metal 147,112 t

nodes.name: Other ferrosilicon suppliers and traders (e.g., Elkem, Brazilian and Malaysian producers)
nodes.description: Imported ferrosilicon. Ferroglobe reported a favorable final US antidumping decision on ferrosilicon in Q1 2025, which shrinks this channel.

nodes.name: MgO annealing-separator and insulation-coating suppliers (e.g., Tateho Chemical)
nodes.description: High-purity magnesium oxide (boron- and chlorine-controlled) for the high-temperature box anneal, plus phosphate and colloidal-silica insulation coatings. Tateho holds patents in this field. US suppliers to Cliffs are not identified.

nodes.name: Electricity and gas suppliers to Butler PA and Zanesville OH
nodes.description: Grid power (PJM) for the EAF, rolling and finishing, plus natural gas for decarburization and box annealing. GOES is among the most energy-intensive flat steels.

nodes.name: Ferroboron, silicon and high-purity iron suppliers to Metglas
nodes.description: Inputs for Fe-B-Si amorphous ribbon: low-residual iron, ferroboron (~3 wt% B) and silicon. Suppliers not identified; ferroboron is largely imported (assumption).

nodes.name: Cleveland-Cliffs (Butler Works PA, Zanesville OH)
nodes.description: The only US (and North American) GOES producer. Butler melts and rolls, and Zanesville finishes. A $170M project (with a $75M DOE grant) adds ~25% GOES output by 2028. Cliffs discloses no GOES tonnage or price.
nodes.size_label: Stainless + electrical shipments 552k net tons (2025); GOES revenue est. $0.5-0.95B

nodes.name: Nippon Steel
nodes.description: Leading global maker of high-grade GOES. Commerce found Japan was the main GOES source for Canadian and Mexican core makers, and Japan and Korea led direct US coil imports in 2019. Nippon Steel owns U.S. Steel (since 2025), which makes no GOES.
nodes.size_label: US-bound GOES (direct + via MX/CA cores) est. $115-300M/yr

nodes.name: JFE Steel
nodes.description: Second Japanese GOES producer. It is assumed to share Japan's role as a supplier to North American core makers. Company-level US volumes are not disclosed.

nodes.name: POSCO
nodes.description: Korean GOES producer. Korea was a leading origin of direct US GOES coil imports in 2019 (Commerce).

nodes.name: China Baowu (Baosteel)
nodes.description: World's largest GOES producer. Its North American role is inferred: Cliffs says Canadian and Mexican core makers use steel melted outside North America. US tariff and EO exposure limits direct sales.

nodes.name: thyssenkrupp Electrical Steel
nodes.description: European GOES producer (plus India) of high-permeability grades used in power transformers. Assumed to be a minor supplier of US coil.

nodes.name: Metglas (Proterial)
nodes.description: The only US amorphous-ribbon producer (Conway SC). It doubled its HB1M line in 2023. It historically exports most of its output; amorphous holds ~2% of the US distribution market.
nodes.ownership: Proterial Ltd. (Bain Capital-owned, formerly Hitachi Metals)

nodes.name: Chinese amorphous ribbon/core producers (e.g., Qingdao Yunlu, AT&M)
nodes.description: POWER reports the US relies on amorphous imports from China. The company names are illustrative, from background knowledge.

nodes.name: Worthington Steel (Tempel)
nodes.description: Largest merchant lamination and core maker in North America (assessment). Tempel was bought for $255M in 2021. The new Burlington ON plant (~US$85M, opened Jun 24, 2026) doubles transformer-core output. Since Jun 3, 2026, Worthington also controls Klöckner & Co (~62%).

nodes.name: Corefficient (Kloeckner Metals)
nodes.description: Monterrey-based maker of step-lap mitred and wound distribution cores selling into the US, Canada and Mexico. It is part of Kloeckner Metals, so it is now likely under Worthington Steel's control after the Klöckner deal (inference).
nodes.ownership: Kloeckner Metals / Klöckner & Co (~62% Worthington Steel since Jun 2026)

nodes.name: Other Mexican and Canadian core and lamination makers
nodes.description: Smaller core shops in Mexico and Canada that export cores and laminations to US builders. Canada (52%) and Mexico (45%) supplied >95% of US core imports in 2019.

nodes.name: US merchant core makers and GOES slitters (e.g., MK Magnetics, Magnetic Metals)
nodes.description: US independents that slit GOES and make wound or stacked cores for smaller builders and rebuilders. The names come from supplier directories and their capabilities are not verified.

nodes.name: In-house core shops at integrated North American builders
nodes.description: Captive slitting, cutting and core-building lines at Howard, ERMCO, Prolec GE, Hitachi Energy, Eaton, Siemens Energy and others. They buy GOES coil, mostly from Cliffs. Surveyed builders imported ~75% of wound cores and 54% of stacked cores in 2019, so captive lines cover the rest.

nodes.name: ERMCO

chain_research.notes:
Key facts (sourced):
- Cleveland-Cliffs (Butler PA, Zanesville OH) is the only North American GOES mill. Its 2025 stainless-plus-electrical shipments were 552k net tons, out of 16.2M total. Cliffs discloses no GOES tonnage or price. Butler adds ~25% GOES output by 2028 ($170M project with a $75M DOE grant). A reported DoD contract worth up to $400M for domain-refined GOES runs to 2030 (secondary source, not verified) and competes for Butler output.
- In 2019, direct GOES coil imports were ~27k MT (mainly Japan and Korea), plus ~68k MT embedded in imported laminations and cores. That put import reliance at ~44% (Commerce Section 232 report; Payne Institute).
- US core imports rose from $22M (2015) to $167M (2019), with Canada at 52% and Mexico at 45%. A secondary analysis puts them at $126M (2018) and $524M (2025). Cliffs' inclusion request says Canada and Mexico laminations and cores rose 321% from 2018 to 2024.
- DOE's 2024 rule keeps ~75% of distribution core steel in GOES, against ~225k MT of domestic distribution electrical-steel demand. Metglas has ~45k t of capacity.

Computed estimates (labelled est.):
- 2019 US GOES consumption ≈ (27k+68k)/0.44 ≈ 216k MT.
- 2025E consumption is 220-320k MT including steel inside imported cores. At $4-6k/MT that is about $1.0-1.9B.
- Cliffs: 120-160k MT, about $0.5-0.95B, or roughly 45-55% of tonnage. One secondary source claims only 20% of demand is met domestically.
- North American core market (merchant plus captive): about $1.1-2.5B. Merchant cores are about $0.4-0.85B, of which Tempel is the largest.

Caveats:
- No public US GOES price index exists. The anchors run $3.9-7.5k per short ton, and European import averages in 2025 were $2.4-3.5k/MT (gtaic, weak).
- Mill-to-core-maker pairings, apart from the Cliffs-to-integrated-builders link, are inferred. They rest on Commerce's finding that Japan is the main source for Mexican and Canadian core makers and on Cliffs' claim that those core makers use non-North American melt.
- The duty on cores is unresolved (25% or 50%). CRS says 50% was extended to distribution cores and laminations on Aug 15, 2025.
- Worthington Steel took control of Klöckner & Co (~62%) on Jun 3, 2026. Corefficient is a Kloeckner Metals unit, so it is likely now under Worthington. Worthington also booked impairments in its Electrical Steel reporting unit in FY2026.
- S3 flows count only the share attributable to GOES. Butler's EAF route and the Toledo HBI link are assumptions.

Sources: CLF 10-K https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/764065/000076406526000025/clf-20251231.htm; Commerce https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/11/18/2021-24958/; Payne https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/grain-oriented-electrical-steel-in-u-s-commercial-and-military-supply-chains/; POWER https://www.powermag.com/doe-eases-requirements-in-final-transformer-efficiency-standards-amid-supply-chain-strain/

nodes.name: Freeport-McMoRan North America copper mines

nodes.name: Rio Tinto Kennecott

nodes.name: Imported refined copper (Chile, Peru, Canada, Mexico)

nodes.name: Bauxite and alumina suppliers
nodes.description: Alumina feeds US and Canadian smelters, roughly 2 t of alumina per t of aluminum. Sources include Alcoa's own refineries, Century's majority-owned Jamalco (Jamaica) and third-party alumina.

nodes.name: Softwood pulpwood growers and timber owners
nodes.description: Long-fibre softwood is the raw material for the unbleached kraft pulp in transformerboard and insulating paper. Nordic and North American forests supply it.

nodes.name: Naphthenic crude oil suppliers
nodes.description: Imported and Gulf Coast low-wax naphthenic crudes run by Ergon (Vicksburg MS, historically barged from Ergon's St. James LA terminal), Calumet (Shreveport/Princeton LA) and Cross Oil. The crude sources are not publicly itemized.

nodes.name: US soybean growers
nodes.description: US farm soybeans crushed into the soybean oil used for natural-ester dielectric fluid (FR3).

nodes.name: Freeport-McMoRan El Paso refinery and rod mills
nodes.description: The El Paso TX refinery turns Miami smelter anode into cathode. Rod mills in El Paso TX and Miami AZ convert own and purchased cathode into continuous-cast rod for wire makers.

nodes.name: Asarco (Grupo Mexico)
nodes.description: US subsidiary of Grupo Mexico with Arizona mines and the Amarillo TX copper refinery and rod plant. It sells cathode and rod into the US wire industry.

nodes.name: Southwire Company (copper rod)
nodes.description: Largest US copper rod producer, running an SCR continuous-cast mill in Carrollton GA. Southwire specifies LME Grade A cathode for magnet-wire rod.

nodes.name: Alcoa
nodes.description: Integrated aluminum producer with US and Quebec smelters, supplying primary metal to North American rolling mills and conductor makers.

nodes.name: Century Aluminum
nodes.description: The largest US-owned primary aluminum smelter operator (Mt. Holly SC, Sebree KY). Holds a majority stake in the Jamalco alumina refinery.

nodes.name: Rio Tinto Aluminium (Quebec smelters)
nodes.description: Quebec hydro-powered smelters, part of the Canadian supply that makes up most US primary aluminum imports.

nodes.name: Electrical-grade kraft pulp and insulating paper mills
nodes.description: Unbleached softwood kraft pulp for transformerboard, plus insulating kraft, crepe and thermally upgraded papers. Much of it is imported from Nordic mills. No named supplier to North American converters was confirmed.

nodes.name: US soybean crushers and refiners (Cargill, ADM, Bunge)
nodes.description: Crush soybeans into refined oil. Cargill's own crush is the likely main feedstock for its FR3 fluid.

nodes.name: Essex Solutions (formerly Essex Furukawa Magnet Wire)
nodes.description: Largest North American magnet-wire maker. It reshaped its Simcoe ON plant to add CTC lines for energy-market (transformer) customers. Superior Essex (LS Cable) bought out Furukawa in April 2024 and renamed the business in 2025.

nodes.name: Rea Magnet Wire (Elektrisola)

chain_research.notes:
Scale (all estimates unless noted): North American transformer builders buy roughly $2.0-4.5B a year of the conductors, insulation and fluids in this slice. That splits into about $1.0-2.0B of copper conductor, $0.12-0.3B of aluminum winding, $0.4-1.0B of insulation and $0.3-0.85B of fluids. The base for the shares is an assumed NA builder output of $16-22B for 2026. Research firms put the US transformer market alone at ~$13.8B in 2025 (MarketsandMarkets, W).

Copper tonnage (computed, W):
- Distribution: 120-200 GVA/yr, ~50% copper-wound, 0.5-0.7 t/MVA (a 500 kVA unit holds ~290-360 kg per a vendor source) = 35-65 kt.
- Power: 100-180 GVA at 0.1-0.25 t/MVA (JRC: 45-50 t per large unit) = 15-35 kt.
- Dry-type: 5-10 kt.
- Total: ~55-110 kt. At Sep-2026 LME of $14,474/t (+45% YoY) plus a $2-5k/t fabrication premium, that is $0.9-2.1B.
- Copper wire PPI is +19% YoY. Section 232 puts 50% on semi-finished copper and will put 15% then 30% on refined cathode (2027-28), so domestic rod and cathode sourcing is becoming a cost lever.

Fluids: research firms size the NA transformer-oil market at $563M (2024) and the US market at $512M (2025), both W. Ergon's +$2.05/gal and the +111% base-stock PPI imply 2026 spend well above that. New-fill volume is a computed 60-110M gal.

Facts found this round:
- Essex is now Essex Solutions, 100% Superior Essex/LS Cable since Apr 2024; it is adding CTC capacity at Simcoe ON.
- Sam Dong is expanding CTC in TN ($13.5M) and OF rod in OH (to 14M lb/month).
- Hitachi closed Canduct on Jul 2, 2026.
- Weidmann's VT expansion (+30% transformerboard) opened May 27, 2026.
- Arclin closed its purchase of DuPont's Nomex business on Apr 1, 2026.
- Cargill's 2026 FR3 expansions are in Europe and Turkiye, with no North American expansion found.
- Ergon Vicksburg runs 26,500 bpd, with +20% crude capacity due Q1 2027.

Caveats:
- No supplier-to-builder contract was confirmed. Every named edge is an inference labelled likely or plausible.
- Market shares are assumptions.
- Encore Wire (Prysmian) makes rod mainly for its own building wire, so it was left out as a magnet-wire supplier.
- Novelis, Granges and JW Aluminum were not confirmed as transformer-strip suppliers.
- Builder winding scrap (~3-8% of wire) flows back to scrap dealers and is not modeled.
- Hitachi's fluid supplier was not identified.
- The values on mine, crude and soybean edges are only the transformer-attributable share of much larger flows.

chain_research.notes:
Market frame (all est.): North American transformer builders sell ~$18-24B a year, about $7-10B in power and substation units (>=10 MVA, including importers' NA deliveries) and $11-15B in distribution, pad-mount and dry-type. The basis is a sum of named makers: Prolec GE's implied ~$2.7-3.0B revenue (computed from $9,656M at 12.9-14.1x 2025E EBITDA and ~25% margin), Forgent $1.42B, Hammond ~C$1.3B run-rate, and others assumed. Vendor cost guides (weak) put tank and structure at 10-15% of a power unit's price, radiators at 3-5%, bushings at 2-4%, and OLTC plus accessories at 5-12%. On that basis, builder spend on tanks is ~$1.4-3.0B (mostly made in-house; outsourced ~$170-800M), bushings ~$0.25-0.6B, OLTCs ~$0.3-0.45B in NA (global market ~$1.8B, weak), radiators ~$0.2-0.5B, coatings ~$55-170M and steel plate and sheet ~$0.2-0.6B. Blasting abrasives are trivial at ~$2-8M.

Structure:
- Reinhausen dominates OLTCs and is expanding Humboldt TN.
- Hitachi is the most integrated builder: Alamo bushings (>$100M, largest NA bushing site), its own tap changers, and Canduct.
- Trench's >$60M Charlotte plant (opened Jul 2026; 3,500 bushings/yr, room for 10,000) is the main new merchant bushing supply, and the source an entrant would use.
- Qualitrol (Ralliant, double-digit 2025 growth) and Doble (~$318M FY25, computed) earn most of their revenue from utilities, not builders.
- Logistics runs 3-20% of an LPT's cost. Heavy haul and rigging across NA is est. $0.3-1.3B a year, and imports at ports dominate the moves. A Schnabel-car shortage is claimed only by weak sources.
- Service and reman are consolidating: TJC is buying Sunbelt Solomon (pending; financial terms not disclosed), and IPS bought Belyea HV.

For an entrant (FAM):
- Tanks, radiators and field installation are where a mid-size industrial could make or buy capability. Most incumbents fabricate tanks in-house, but importers and new entrants need outside tanks and US field crews.
- Bushings and OLTCs are concentrated, so secure Trench or Reinhausen allocation early.

Caveats:
- Most dollar values are estimates. Only Doble (ESCO), the Trench and Hitachi plant figures, Reinhausen's capacity steps and Sunbelt's scale come from sources.
- Cost-share data comes from Chinese vendor blogs (weak).
- No named tank-fabricator or radiator contracts with specific builders were found, and Menk's NA presence is unverified.
- The Reinhausen, Qualitrol and Sunbelt revenues are undisclosed.
- GOES, cores, copper magnet wire, insulating fluids and pressboard are excluded; another slice covers them.

chain_research.notes:
Key facts found:
- EIA: line-transformer capex by major utilities rose 23% to $7.5B in 2023. Distribution substation equipment was $6.1B, and transmission capex was $27.7B.
- EEI: IOU capex was ~$204B in 2025 and ~$239B in 2026 (secondary).
- EIA 2024 retail revenue was $514.4B: residential $244.4B, commercial $185.0B, industrial $84.1B. 2025 retail kWh: residential 1.51T, commercial 1.49T, industrial 1.04T.
- Data centers used ~312.6 TWh in 2025 (Energy Institute via secondary) and drove ~50% of 2025 demand growth.
- Distributors: Wesco's UBS segment had 2025 sales of $5.5B (-4.9%), hit by public-power weakness including transformer inventory normalization. Wesco's total was $23.5B, Sonepar NA $18.8B and Graybar $12.9B (not modelled; small utility-transformer share).
- Duke: $17.2B annual sourcing, ~$1B with NC suppliers, including GE Vernova transformers from Goldsboro.
- AEP: $72B 2026-30 plan, an EHV transformer development services agreement with Quanta, and an approved 500-765 kV vendor list (Hitachi, HICO, SMIT, Siemens).
- Oncor: $47.5B 2026-30 plan, with LPTs secured and first deliveries in Q1 2027.

Method: no utility discloses its transformer spend. I set IOU transformer purchases at 3.5-6% of capex. That is EIA's 2023 line-transformer capex plus an assumed transformer share of substation equipment, over ~$167B of 2023 IOU capex, net of capitalized installation, cross-checked against Duke's sourcing at 4-7%. Applied to $239B, all IOUs buy est. $8.4-14.3B a year. The eight named IOUs are ~43% of IOU capex.

Not found, so estimated: public power, co-op and TVA totals, and revenue for ERMCO, Border States, RESCO and Gresco.

Caveats:
- Distributor edges are pass-through: a builder's sale to Wesco and Wesco's sale to a muni are the same transformers. Do not sum builder-to-distributor and distributor-to-utility edges.
- Data-center direct buys and EPC-procured units overlap partly.
- "Other builders" is a residual node, not a company.
- C2-to-C3 edges are valued at electricity-cost content only. They are not the revenue of those services.
- Supplier-side cross-check: estimated buyer totals of ~$16-30B/yr exceed visible builder revenues plus imports (~$15-20B), so the upper ends are likely high.
- The JEA bid totals are multi-year bids, not awards.
- Utility revenue splits by customer class are my estimates, not from filings.

edges.basis: Est. 8-12 GW/yr of wind, solar and storage builds multiplied by $40-90k of transformer content per MW (assumed). A vendor guide prices 50-100 MVA step-up units at ~$10-25k/MVA. NextEra says it has purchased transformers through 2030, and its 10 GW gas program adds GSUs from ~2028.

edges.product: GSUs, collector-substation and MV step-up transformers

edges.basis: Est. 2.5-4 GW/yr of US builds multiplied by $40-90k per MW (assumed).

edges.basis: Est. 1.5-3 GW/yr of solar, storage and gas builds multiplied by $40-90k per MW (assumed).

edges.product: Unit-substation, substation and GSU transformers for LNG, refining, chemicals, mining, fabs and oilfield electrification
edges.basis: Est.: an 8-12% industrial and oil and gas share of an assumed $18-30B/yr US transformer market. Both the share and the market size are assumptions, not found figures.

edges.product: Leased AI data-center capacity, Abilene TX Stargate campus (~1.2 GW)
edges.basis: Background knowledge, not re-checked this run: the Crusoe-built campus is owned by a JV with Blue Owl and Primary Digital and leased to Oracle for OpenAI. 2026 rent est. at 0.4-1.0 GW energized multiplied by $1.3-1.8M/MW-yr.

edges.product: GPU cloud capacity
edges.basis: Microsoft was ~62% of CoreWeave's 2024 revenue (S-1, background knowledge), and its share is falling as OpenAI and Meta ramp. Microsoft also contracted Nebius for $17.4B (up to $19.4B) through 2031.

edges.product: GPU cloud capacity
edges.basis: Contract of up to $14.2B through Dec 2031 (Sep 2025), later expanded to ~$21B. 2026 value is a ramp estimate.

edges.product: Solar and storage PPAs (~2.5 GW, 13 projects, online 2026-28)
edges.basis: Value at full operation: 2.5 GW at a ~25-30% capacity factor gives ~5.5-6.5 TWh/yr, priced at an assumed $30-60/MWh. 2026 revenue will be lower.

edges.product: Azure compute for training and inference
edges.basis: Incremental $250B Azure commitment from the Oct 2025 recapitalization (est. 2025-30), plus earlier commitments. The 2026 share is sized from OpenAI's ~$40B run-rate and reported ~$14B 2026 loss.

edges.product: OCI compute (Stargate)
edges.basis: ~$300B over ~5 years starting 2027, as reported by the WSJ and never confirmed by the companies. The 2026 value reflects the Abilene ramp.

edges.product: EC2 Nvidia GPU capacity
edges.basis: $38B seven-year agreement (Nov 2025) with full capacity by end-2026, an average of ~$5.4B/yr.

edges.product: GPU cloud capacity
edges.basis: Contracts total ~$22.4B (Mar-Sep 2025), later raised by up to $65B. The 2026 delivery value is estimated.

edges.product: TPU cloud capacity
edges.basis: Oct 2025 deal: up to 1M TPUs, with >1 GW online in 2026. A further multi-GW TPU deal (Apr 2026, with Broadcom) starts in 2027. 2026 est. at 0.4-0.8 GW average multiplied by ~$10-12B per GW-year (assumed).

edges.product: Trainium capacity (Project Rainier) and AWS cloud
edges.basis: Anthropic names AWS its primary cloud and training partner, but the value is not disclosed. Sized from Anthropic's $30-65B run-rate and an assumed compute intensity.

edges.basis: $30B Azure compute commitment covering up to 1 GW plus an option (Nov 2025). 2026 value is a ramp estimate.

edges.product: Retail colocation and interconnection (Americas)
edges.basis: 2026 revenue ~$10.2-10.3B, implied by the 11-12% growth guide, multiplied by an assumed ~42-46% Americas share.

edges.product: Cloud services (IaaS and PaaS) to North American enterprises
edges.basis: AWS 2026E revenue ~$150-160B (assumed ~20% growth; not sourced this run) multiplied by an assumed ~55-60% North America share, less the AI-lab contracts.

edges.product: Azure cloud services to North American enterprises
edges.basis: Azure passed $75B in FY25 (background knowledge), and FY26E is ~$100B. Multiplied by an assumed ~50% North America share, less OpenAI and Anthropic.

edges.product: Google Cloud services to North American enterprises
edges.basis: Google Cloud 2026E ~$75-85B (assumed) multiplied by an assumed ~50% North America share, less Anthropic and Meta.

edges.product: Contracted power from wind, solar, storage, nuclear and gas
edges.basis: NEER revenue est. $8-10B (background knowledge, not re-checked). It contracted a record 4 GW in Q1 2026 and has a ~33 GW backlog. Offtakers include hyperscalers.

edges.product: Contracted wind, solar, storage and gas power, incl. a ~800 MW Meta deal
edges.basis: Private company. Est. 15-20 GW of operating US capacity multiplied by $100-175k/MW-yr of revenue (assumed).

edges.product: Contracted solar and storage power to utilities and hyperscalers
edges.basis: Est. ~10-14 GW of contracted US renewables and storage multiplied by $120-180k/MW-yr (assumed).

edges.product: ChatGPT consumer subscriptions (North America)
edges.basis: ~$40B run-rate (Aug 2026, Bloomberg via secondary) multiplied by an assumed 55-65% consumer share and 35-45% North America share.

edges.product: ChatGPT Enterprise, Team and API (North America)
edges.basis: ~$40B run-rate multiplied by an assumed 35-45% business and API share and 45-60% North America share.

edges.product: Claude API, enterprise seats and Claude Code (North America, incl. resale via cloud marketplaces)
edges.basis: Run-rate $30B (early 2026) to $65B (mid-2026); sources conflict. Multiplied by an assumed 80-90% business share and 50-60% North America share. Anthropic books cloud-resold revenue gross.

chain_research.notes:
Hyperscaler capex, 2026 guidance (secondary sources, revised often): Amazon ~$200B incl. Amazon Leo, Alphabet $195-205B, Microsoft ~$190B (CY26), Meta $125-145B and Oracle $90-95B gross. That is ~$800-835B with Oracle, and ~$700-725B for the big four (+~77% YoY).

Transformer content per MW of IT load (computed estimate):
- MV/LV unit-substation transformers: $36-135k (1.2-2.7 MVA installed at N+1 to 2N, at $30-50/kVA).
- HV/MV main-substation units: $20-78k (9-22 units/GW at $15-30k/MVA).
- Optional EHV interconnect units: up to ~$50k.
- Total: ~$0.06-0.26M/MW; edges use $0.08-0.20M.
- That is only ~3-10% of the data-center electrical stack, which BofA (via Eaton) puts at ~$2.1M/MW for UPS, generators, switchgear and PDUs. It is under 1.5% of the ~$17.6M/MW all-in build cost excluding chips (Cushman & Wakefield; power infrastructure ~21%). Transformers are the bottleneck, not the budget.

Capacity:
- CBRE: 7.5 GW under construction in primary markets (H1 2026).
- BNEF: 15.9 GW of US IT capacity under construction (Sep 2025).
- JLL: 66 GW broad North American pipeline.
- Jefferies: only 12 of 24 GW scheduled for 2026 is under construction.
- At 12-20 GW/yr, North American data-center electrical equipment spend is ~$24-60B/yr (central ~$35-45B) and transformer spend ~$1-4.5B/yr (central ~$2B). The buyer-level edges sum to ~12-21 GW and ~$0.9-4.2B.

Caveats:
1. Direct hyperscaler transformer buying is documented only as orders from unnamed 'US big tech' buyers: Hyosung $287M, LS Electric ~$247M, HD Hyundai ~KRW 1.1T. These overlap the per-hyperscaler estimates, so do not add them. Named-maker flows (Prolec GE, Forgent, Schneider) also overlap the 'maker not disclosed' aggregate.
2. Per-company GW, the per-MW transformer content, renewable content of $40-90k/MW and the industrial market share are assumptions.
3. Cloud and AI-lab flows are 2026 estimates carved out of multi-year contract totals. Oracle-OpenAI's $300B is WSJ-reported and starts in 2027. Anthropic run-rate figures conflict, and Anthropic books cloud-resold revenue gross.
4. Not re-checked this run (background knowledge): Crusoe's Abilene lease to Oracle; Vantage's Stargate sites; CoreWeave's 62% Microsoft share; Alphabet's purchase of Intersect; NEER revenue; AWS, Azure and Google Cloud revenue bases.
5. xAI reportedly imported Chinese three-phase transformers and used a medium-voltage design to bypass the large-power-transformer queue. This is relevant to EO 14421 exposure.
6. No developer reservation of transformer capacity with a named maker was found. NextEra says it has purchased transformers through 2030.

nodes.name: Naphthenic crude oil suppliers

nodes.name: Other IOUs and transmission companies (Southern, Oncor, Dominion, Xcel, FPL, PG&E, others)
nodes.description: Remaining IOUs and transcos. EEI puts 2026 IOU capex at $239B; transformer buying est. 3.5-6% of capex. Oncor has secured Permian LPTs (first deliveries Q1 2027); Dominion adds substation units for NoVA data centers; Xcel cites transformer delays.

nodes.name: Public power and federal utilities (munis, JEA, Austin Energy, TVA, WAPA, BPA)
nodes.description: ~2,000 municipal utilities and state authorities plus TVA and federal PMAs. Buy substation units directly and distribution units through bids (JEA FY26-29, Austin Energy $200M NTE) and distributors.

nodes.name: Electric cooperatives
nodes.description: ~830 distribution and ~60 G&T co-ops owning ~42% of US distribution lines; buy through co-op-owned ERMCO and distributors such as RESCO and Border States.

nodes.name: Wesco International (incl. Anixter)
nodes.description: Largest US electrical distributor; resells transformers to utilities (incl. Sourcewell) and dry-type units to contractors. Public-power transformer sales fell in 2025 on inventory normalization.

nodes.name: Sonepar North America (Stuart C. Irby)
nodes.description: Irby resells GE/Prolec and other transformers to munis and IOUs (JEA, Austin Energy, Zeeland awards); Sonepar's electrical branches sell dry-type units.

nodes.name: Other distributors (Border States, RESCO, Gresco, Graybar, CED)
nodes.description: Regional utility-supply and electrical distributors that resell distribution and dry-type units to munis, co-ops, contractors and industrial buyers; frequent bidders on municipal tenders.

nodes.name: Data-center developers, colos, neoclouds and their EPCs
nodes.description: QTS, Vantage, Crusoe, CoreWeave, Equinix, Digital Realty, Stack, Aligned and others, plus EPCs procuring for hyperscaler self-builds. Buy main-substation, MV/LV pad-mount and dry-type units (~$0.08-0.20M of transformers per MW).

nodes.name: NextEra Energy Resources
nodes.description: Largest US renewables and storage developer (~33 GW backlog; record 4 GW contracted Q1 2026). Says it has purchased transformers through 2030; up to 10 GW of gas from ~2028.

nodes.name: Other generation developers and EPCs (Invenergy, AES, Intersect, RWE, gas IPPs)
nodes.description: IPPs and their EPCs (Blattner, Mortenson, Kiewit, Primoris) buying GSUs, collector-substation and MV step-up units for solar, wind, BESS and gas; ~50-160 US GSUs/yr from the gas-turbine backlog.

nodes.name: Industrial, LNG and oil and gas buyers
nodes.description: LNG terminals, refineries, chemicals, mining, semiconductor and battery fabs, and Permian electrification buying unit-substation, substation and GSU units directly or via EPCs.

nodes.name: Microsoft
nodes.description: Leases and rents much of its capacity (CoreWeave, Nebius) besides self-built campuses; sells Azure compute to OpenAI and Anthropic.
nodes.size_label: CY2026 capex ~$190B; self-build transformer content est. $80-400M/yr

nodes.name: Alphabet (Google)
nodes.description: Mostly self-builds; sells TPU capacity to Anthropic. Agreed to buy Intersect Power (background knowledge).

nodes.name: Amazon (AWS)
nodes.description: Mostly self-builds; Anthropic's primary cloud and training partner and a $38B OpenAI supplier.

nodes.name: Meta Platforms
nodes.description: Self-builds gigawatt campuses, rents from CoreWeave and buys solar and storage PPAs from NextEra and Invenergy.

nodes.name: Oracle (OCI)
nodes.description: Builds OpenAI's Stargate capacity mainly through leased campuses (e.g., Crusoe's Abilene TX).

nodes.name: Hyperscalers and AI campuses unnamed in transformer orders
nodes.description: Direct transformer orders disclosed only as from 'US big tech' (Hyosung $287M, HD Hyundai ~$721M framework, LS Electric ~$247M). Buyers are among the named hyperscalers, xAI and AI labs; shown separately to avoid guessing.

nodes.name: US residential electricity customers
nodes.description: ~145M household accounts; 1.51T kWh in 2025.

nodes.name: US commercial electricity customers (incl. many data centers)
nodes.description: Offices, retail, hospitals, schools and data centers billed as commercial; 1.49T kWh in 2025. Data centers used ~312.6 TWh in 2025.

nodes.name: US industrial electricity customers
nodes.description: Manufacturing, mining and process industry; 1.04T kWh in 2025.

nodes.name: OpenAI
nodes.description: Rents compute from Microsoft, Oracle, AWS and CoreWeave rather than owning most data centers.

nodes.name: Anthropic
nodes.description: Rents compute from AWS (primary), Google TPUs and Microsoft Azure.

nodes.name: Enterprises renting cloud and colocation (North America)
nodes.description: Companies and public bodies buying IaaS/PaaS and colocation, excluding AI-lab mega-contracts. LBNL projects data centers at up to 11.8% of US electricity by 2030.

nodes.name: Household final demand (incl. EVs, heat pumps)
nodes.description: Household consumption of electricity-dependent goods and services, including electrification of transport and heating.

nodes.name: Demand for US-made goods (reshoring)
nodes.description: Buyers of domestically made goods, including new fabs, battery plants and process industry that pull industrial load.

network_draft.notes:
Scale: 101 nodes (S3 11, S2 15, S1 24, B 25, C1 12, C2 9, C3 5; 7 Fulton). 128 flow edges and 12 fulton_opportunity edges. Every edge was checked by script: all ids exist, all layer pairs are allowed, there are no duplicate pairs and no isolated nodes. B->C2 edges go only to the unnamed-hyperscaler node.

Merges:
- Cliffs GOES and Cliffs carbon sheet are one node; Cliffs mining and Toledo HBI are one node.
- Corefficient is folded into Worthington-Tempel (Worthington has controlled ~62% of Klöckner since Jun 2026).
- Canduct is folded into Hitachi components.
- Niagara is folded into PTT (both Quanta).
- IPS/Belyea is in the reman aggregate; Eaglerise and Kerec/Sungjin/Taihan are in distribution imports; Schneider is in other dry-type.
- JFE, Baowu, thyssenkrupp and Metglas are in other GOES; Asarco is in Grupo Mexico; Rea, imported CTC and aluminum strip are in other conductors.
- Southern, Oncor, Dominion, Xcel, FPL and PG&E are in other IOUs; JEA, Austin Energy, TVA and WAPA are in public power; QTS, Vantage, Crusoe and CoreWeave are in DC developers.
- Every builder catch-all from the supplier slices was reallocated to named builders. Those splits are assumptions.

Sanity checks:
- Builder outflows sum to $13.1-23.6B (midpoint ~$18.4B), against the builders slice's ~$20B bottom-up and the $20-30B anchor. The midpoint sits at the low end because reactors and switchgear were trimmed from HD Hyundai and Hyosung, and industrial direct buys are only partly modelled.
- Prolec edges total $2.1-3.25B (anchor ~$3B).
- Forgent transformer edges total $0.4-0.68B, inside its $1.42B FY26 revenue.
- Hyosung $287M is annualized to $95-145M/yr.
- HD Hyundai, Hyosung and LS sell a combined $1.5-2.3B into NA, against $738M of Korean >10 MVA exports. That implies most of their supply comes from Montgomery and Memphis, so these figures are at the high end.
- Cliffs is the only domestic GOES source; all other GOES is imported.

Double counting:
- Distributor resale to munis and co-ops (C1 to C1) is not drawn. Distributor C1->C2 edges carry only C&I resale.
- The unnamed-hyperscaler node overlaps the named hyperscalers. Those have no transformer edges; their self-build transformer content is in size_label.
- C1->C2 and C2->C3 values are electricity or compute revenue, not transformer dollars, and are 10-100x larger. Scale them separately in the UI.
- S3 values are transformer-attributable shares only. Hitachi components and Cliffs HBI are captive transfers.

Dropped because of layer rules:
- Doble and Qualitrol utility retrofits (S1->C1).
- The recycler loop (C1->S1).
- CoreWeave->OpenAI (C1->C3).
- Cathode to Sam Dong (S3->S1).

Fulton:
- Excluded: Imperial Zinc (galvanizing, outside the transformer chain), Mayco (lead), Setna iO (aviation) and ZYCI (weak link).
- Largest opportunities: Imperial copper loop $60-220M, Transend $40-120M, AFCO $20-70M, Imperial Aluminum $15-60M. Metaltec is small ($1.5-5M) but a direct consumable.

All values are estimates. FX assumed at 1,400 KRW, 7.2 RMB and 1.37 CAD per USD.

nodes.name: Cleveland-Cliffs iron ore and Toledo HBI
nodes.description: Captive Minnesota/Michigan pellet mines and the Toledo hot-briquetted iron plant. HBI is assumed (not verified) to supply part of the Butler EAF charge for GOES.
nodes.size_label: Toledo nameplate 1.6M t/yr HBI; GOES-attributable flow est. $12-32M

nodes.name: Ferrous scrap processors and transformer dismantlers
nodes.description: Scrap processors (incl. Cliffs-owned FPT), pig iron importers and transformer recyclers (A-Line, TCI of Ohio, Sunbelt's ~1,000 units/day). Supply low-residual metallics to EAF mills.
nodes.size_label: Transformer-derived recovered metal est. $100-350M/yr (all metals); the GOES-melt scrap edge is general scrap, not transformer-derived

nodes.name: Ferroglobe
nodes.description: Largest US ferrosilicon and silicon-metal producer (Beverly OH, Calvert City KY). GOES carries ~3% Si added as ferrosilicon; supply to Cliffs is inferred.

nodes.name: Imported ferrosilicon, MgO and coating chemicals
nodes.description: Imported FeSi (Elkem, Brazil, Malaysia; limited by the 2025 AD case), high-purity MgO annealing separator (e.g., Tateho) and phosphate/colloidal-silica insulation coatings for GOES.

nodes.name: Freeport-McMoRan Arizona copper mines
nodes.description: Morenci, Bagdad, Safford and others feed the Miami AZ smelter; anode is refined at El Paso.

nodes.name: Rio Tinto Kennecott
nodes.description: Integrated Bingham Canyon mine, smelter and refinery near Salt Lake City; one of few US sources of mined and refined cathode.

nodes.name: Imported refined copper (Chile, Peru, Canada)
nodes.description: Codelco, Glencore, Teck and others cover a large share of US cathode use. Section 232 refined-copper duty of 15% (2027) and 30% (2028).

nodes.name: Bauxite and alumina suppliers
nodes.description: Alumina for US and Canadian smelters (~2 t per t of aluminum): Alcoa refineries, Century's Jamalco and third-party supply.

nodes.name: Softwood pulpwood and soybeans
nodes.description: Long-fibre softwood for unbleached kraft pulp (transformerboard, insulating paper) and US soybeans crushed for natural-ester FR3 fluid.

nodes.name: Naphthenic crude oil suppliers
nodes.description: Imported and Gulf Coast low-wax naphthenic crudes run by Ergon (Vicksburg MS), Calumet (Shreveport/Princeton LA) and others.

nodes.name: Imperial Recycling (Imperial Group, incl. Midwest Industrial Metals, Exeon Processors)
nodes.description: Fulton's family metals group (founded 1962). Recovers copper and aluminum from insulated, armored and oilfield cable; Midwest Industrial Metals (Northlake IL) buys non-ferrous scrap; Exeon (Jonesboro IN) granulates wire into clean chops; growing PVC jacket recycling.

nodes.name: Cleveland-Cliffs (Butler Works GOES, carbon sheet)
nodes.description: The only US and North American GOES producer (Butler PA melt/roll, Zanesville OH finish); a $170M project ($75M DOE grant) adds ~25% GOES by 2028. Also sells carbon sheet for distribution tanks and cabinets.
nodes.size_label: GOES revenue est. $0.5-0.95B (120-160k MT); 2025 stainless+electrical shipments 552k net tons

nodes.name: Nippon Steel
nodes.description: Leading high-permeability GOES maker; Japan is the main GOES source for Canadian and Mexican core makers and a top origin of direct US coil imports. Owns U.S. Steel (no GOES).

nodes.name: POSCO
nodes.description: Korean GOES producer; Korea was the #2 origin of direct US coil imports (Commerce). Assumed main GOES source for Korean-owned US plants.

nodes.name: Other GOES and amorphous (JFE, Baowu, thyssenkrupp, Metglas)
nodes.description: JFE Steel (Japan), China Baowu (tariff- and EO 14421-limited), thyssenkrupp Electrical Steel, and Metglas (Proterial; Conway SC, ~45 kt/yr amorphous ribbon, mostly exported).

nodes.name: Freeport-McMoRan El Paso refinery and rod mills
nodes.description: Refines Miami smelter anode into cathode and casts continuous rod at El Paso TX and Miami AZ for wire makers.

nodes.name: Southwire (copper rod)
nodes.description: Largest US copper rod producer (SCR mill, Carrollton GA); specifies LME Grade A cathode for magnet-wire rod.

nodes.name: Grupo Mexico copper (Asarco, Southern Copper)
nodes.description: Asarco's Amarillo TX refinery and rod plant plus Southern Copper's Mexican cathode; the assumed domestic source for Mexican magnet-wire makers.

nodes.name: Primary aluminum (Rio Tinto Aluminium, Alcoa, Century)
nodes.description: Quebec hydro smelters (largest source of US primary imports), Alcoa US/Quebec smelters and Century (Mt. Holly SC, Sebree KY) supplying rollers of winding strip and foil.

nodes.name: Electrical-grade kraft pulp and insulating paper mills
nodes.description: Unbleached softwood kraft pulp for transformerboard plus insulating kraft, crepe and thermally upgraded papers; much is imported from Nordic mills.

nodes.name: Nucor (plate mills)
nodes.description: EAF plate mills at Hertford NC, Tuscaloosa AL and Longview TX near the Southeastern transformer cluster; scrap-fed, closing a loop with transformer recycling.

nodes.name: Other plate and sheet mills (SSAB, Steel Dynamics, AM/NS Calvert, Algoma, Ternium)
nodes.description: Hot-rolled, cold-rolled, galvanized sheet and plate for tanks, covers, radiators and enclosures. Names are typical mills, not confirmed suppliers.

nodes.name: Ergon (HyVolt naphthenic transformer oil)
nodes.description: Largest NA naphthenic refiner (Vicksburg MS, Newell WV). Raised naphthenic prices +$2.05/gal in Mar-Apr 2026; $400M Vicksburg expansion (+20% crude) due Q1 2027.

nodes.name: Cargill (Envirotemp FR3 natural ester)
nodes.description: Leading soybean-based natural-ester dielectric fluid, originated at Cooper Power (now Eaton); 100+ US utilities use ester-filled units. 2026 expansions were in Europe and Turkiye only.

nodes.name: Other transformer oils (Nynas, Shell Diala, Calumet)
nodes.description: Nynas Nytro (imported from Europe), Shell Diala inhibited and GTL oils, and Calumet naphthenic grades; weighted to power transformers and global OEMs.

nodes.name: Imperial Aluminum-Minerva and Imperial Alloys (Imperial Group)
nodes.description: Secondary aluminum smelter in Minerva OH converting scrap into die-cast and foundry alloys. Does not make EC-grade (1350) winding aluminum.

nodes.name: Worthington Steel: Tempel and Corefficient
nodes.description: Largest NA merchant core maker. Tempel's Burlington ON plant (~US$85M, opened Jun 2026) doubles transformer-core output; Corefficient (Monterrey) is a Kloeckner Metals unit, likely under Worthington since it took ~62% of Klöckner on Jun 3, 2026.

nodes.name: Other merchant core makers (Mexico, Canada, US)
nodes.description: Smaller Mexican and Canadian core shops (Canada 52%, Mexico 45% of 2019 US core imports) plus US slitters and core makers such as MK Magnetics and Magnetic Metals. US core imports reached ~$524M in 2025 (secondary); that figure also includes Tempel Canada and Corefficient output, shown under Worthington.

nodes.name: Essex Solutions (magnet wire and CTC)
nodes.description: Largest NA magnet-wire maker (ex-Essex Furukawa); reshaped Simcoe ON to add CTC lines for transformer customers.

nodes.name: Sam Dong America / Sam Dong Ohio
nodes.description: Korean-owned conductor maker: $13.5M CTC and enamel expansion at Rogersville TN (Sep 2026) and $13M at Delaware OH lifting oxygen-free rod casting from 5.5M to 14M lb/month.

nodes.name: Magnekon (Viakable / Xignux)
nodes.description: Large Monterrey magnet-wire plant serving transformer and motor makers in Mexico, the US and Canada; sister company of Prolec's former 50% owner Xignux.

nodes.name: Other conductors: imported CTC, Rea/Elektrisola, aluminum strip and foil
nodes.description: Imported CTC and paper-covered conductor (Asta, Korean, Indian, Chinese makers), Rea Magnet Wire (Elektrisola) and aluminum winding strip, foil and wire for distribution units.

nodes.name: Weidmann Electrical Technology
nodes.description: Main NA transformerboard (pressboard) mill and component plant, St. Johnsbury VT; a $40-50M expansion adding >30% capacity opened May 27, 2026.

nodes.name: Other insulation: Arclin Nomex, Krempel, kit converters, imports
nodes.description: Arclin (bought DuPont Aramids, Nomex, ~$1.8B, Apr 1 2026) for dry-type insulation, plus kraft/crepe/DPE paper, laminated wood and pressboard parts from Krempel, converters and imports.

nodes.name: Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen
nodes.description: Dominant on-load tap changer (OLTC) maker; Humboldt TN plant expanded 45% with further OLTC expansion under way; plans to double global capacity by 2030.

nodes.name: Hitachi Energy components (Alamo bushings, tap changers, Canduct)
nodes.description: Alamo TN (>$100M expansion) is becoming NA's largest bushing plant (to 800 kV); plus tap changers and Canduct insulation kits (London ON, Boardman OH; acquired Jul 2, 2026). Mostly captive.

nodes.name: Trench Group (HSP bushings)
nodes.description: Carved out of Siemens Energy in 2024. Its >$60M Charlotte NC plant (25-765 kV bushings, 3,500/yr expandable to 10,000) opened Jul 2026 and is ramping: the main new merchant bushing capacity. Hubbell's PCORE (LeRoy NY) is another US merchant bushing maker; Hitachi's Alamo TN plant is mostly captive.

nodes.name: Qualitrol (Ralliant)
nodes.description: Transformer gauges, pressure relief, temperature monitors and online DGA; >4M grid devices installed. Most monitoring revenue comes from utility retrofits.

nodes.name: Radiators and coolers (Trantech, Menk, imports)
nodes.description: Trantech Radiator Products (leading NA panel-radiator maker) plus imported radiators and forced-oil coolers (Menk, Mexican, Korean, Indian makers).

nodes.name: Independent tank and enclosure fabricators (US, Mexico)
nodes.description: Contract fabricators of tanks, conservators, pad-mount cabinets and structures (e.g., Washington Metal Fabricators, Acero ATD). Most large builders make tanks in-house; importers and new plants outsource.
nodes.size_label: Outsourced est. $170-800M of a $1.4-3.0B tank pool

nodes.name: Coatings (PPG, Sherwin-Williams)
nodes.description: Liquid and powder primer/topcoat systems for tanks, radiators and pad-mount cabinets. Shot-blasting abrasives (Ervin, Metaltec, Winoa) precede painting.

nodes.name: Foundries and machine shops (castings, valves, terminals)
nodes.description: Aluminum and steel castings, bushing flanges, drain and sampling valves, terminal pads, wheels and lifting hardware; fragmented regional suppliers.

nodes.name: Barnhart Crane & Rigging
nodes.description: Heavy-haul and rigging contractor with its own fleet; e.g., moved a 485,500 lb transformer 500+ miles from the Port of Los Angeles to Nevada.

nodes.name: Other heavy haul, rail and ports (Lone Star, Mammoet, Bigge, Emmert, Sarens, Schnabel rail)
nodes.description: Modular-trailer and jack-and-slide moves, Schnabel-car rail (~30 NA cars, weak source) and port handling of imported LPTs. NA heavy-move spend est. $0.3-1.3B.

nodes.name: Field installation contractors (SDMyers, Shermco, OEM crews)
nodes.description: Site assembly, vacuum oil filling and commissioning of new units subcontracted by builders, especially importers without US crews.

nodes.name: Metaltec Steel Abrasive Company
nodes.description: Cast steel shot and grit made from melted scrap (Canton Township MI); one of three leading US abrasive makers. Tanks, radiators and enclosures are shot-blasted before painting.
nodes.ownership: Imperial Group, Lorentzen, Ashland Capital (Fulton, Aug 2022)

nodes.name: Stainless Foundry & Engineering (SFE)
nodes.description: Milwaukee stainless and high-alloy sand and investment castings (to ~200 lb) for energy, nuclear and power-generation OEMs; ~6-week lead times.

nodes.name: AFCO Industries
nodes.description: Aluminum, composite and vinyl building products plus CNC fabrication and contract manufacturing in Alexandria LA, Olive Branch MS, Pell City AL and Olmstead IL. Not a pressure-tight tank shop.
nodes.ownership: Fulton Asset Management and Ashland Capital (closed Jul 31, 2025)

nodes.name: Panther Metalflow
nodes.description: Swiss-type CNC turning and Metalflow zinc cast-in-place assemblies (Walled Lake MI); ISO 9001, ITAR. Could make terminals, studs and bushing hardware.

nodes.name: Transend Logistics
nodes.description: Chicago 3PL and freight broker: flatbed, dry van, drayage, cross-dock and cross-border Mexico-US-Canada lanes. No heavy-haul or Schnabel capability.

nodes.name: Hitachi Energy
nodes.description: Largest LPT supplier into NA: South Boston VA, Crystal Springs MS, Varennes QC plus imports; >$1B US build-out (South Boston $457M 2028-29, Gallman MS $528M 2029). Most vertically integrated (own bushings, tap changers, Canduct).

nodes.name: Siemens Energy (Transformers)
nodes.description: Supplies LPTs and GSUs mainly from Mexico, Brazil and Europe; first US LPT plant, Charlotte NC ($150M, 24-57 units/yr), slipped to 2027.

nodes.name: HD Hyundai Electric
nodes.description: Korean EHV leader with a Montgomery AL plant; plant #2 ($200M, +50% EHV, 765 kV test) due 2027. Q2 2026 operating margin 25.1%.
nodes.size_label: NA revenue ~$1.3-1.7B incl. reactors, switchgear and distribution units (Q2 2026 KRW 541.9B annualized = ~$1.55B); transformer edges est. $0.5-0.9B

nodes.name: Hyosung HICO
nodes.description: Memphis TN plant (ex-Mitsubishi), one of very few US plants building 765 kV units, plus Changwon imports; $208-238M expansions (+50% by 2028). Booked $287M of 765/345 kV orders from two US tech companies (Sep 2026), with deliveries likely in 2027-29.
nodes.size_label: US revenue ~$0.9-1.1B (2025) incl. reactors and breakers

nodes.name: Virginia Transformer Corp (VTC)
nodes.description: Largest US-owned power-transformer maker: 6 NA plants (US, Mexico), ~2-500 MVA. Rincon GA +50% by Mar 2027; holds WAPA's single-award LPT blanket purchase agreement; explored a >$6B sale in 2025.

nodes.name: Pennsylvania Transformer and Niagara (Quanta)
nodes.description: Quanta's transformer units: PTT (5-750 MVA to 765 kV, Canonsburg PA and Raeford NC; pad-mount plant from 2027) and Niagara Power Transformer (Cheektowaga NY; $71.2M expansion). Supports the AEP-Quanta EHV development agreement.

nodes.name: Delta Star

nodes.name: LS Electric
nodes.description: Korean exporter; 2026 US data-center orders of $132M (345 kV) and ~$115M (switchgear and distribution transformers) from unnamed big tech/hyperscalers.

nodes.name: Other imported power transformers (Iljin, Mexican, Brazilian, European, Indian, Turkish)

nodes.name: Prolec GE (GE Vernova)
nodes.description: Largest NA transformer maker (distribution to large power): Monterrey, Goldsboro NC (220 to 420 units/yr by 2027), Shreveport LA, Waukesha WI. GE Vernova took 100% on Feb 2, 2026 ($9,656M total consideration).

nodes.name: WEG Transformers North America
nodes.description: Three Washington MO plants (560 staff) plus Mexico and Brazil; $77M expansion adds 50% of 1-10 MVA capacity.

nodes.name: SGB-SMIT / Southwest Electric
nodes.description: Bought Southwest Electric (Oklahoma City; substation and specialty units) in Mar 2025; imports power units from Europe. On AEP's EHV vendor list.

nodes.name: Eaton (Cooper Power)
nodes.description: Distribution, 3-phase pad-mount, substation and dry-type units from Waukesha WI and Nacogdoches TX; Jonesville SC ($340M, 700 jobs) in 2027. Electrical Americas data-center sales +65% organic.

nodes.name: Howard Industries
nodes.description: Largest US distribution maker (~4,000 staff, 14 MS sites) with in-house core lines; moving up to 250 MVA/345 kV at Ellisville by end-2026.

nodes.name: ERMCO

nodes.name: Central Moloney
nodes.description: Single-phase pole and pad-mount maker (Pine Bluff AR, Panama City Beach FL); sells mostly via distributors such as Border States; JEA FY26-29 awardee.

nodes.name: Forgent Power Solutions (VanTran, MGM)
nodes.description: Listed maker of transformers (VanTran Waco TX, MGM Vernon CA), switchgear and switchboards. FY26 revenue $1.42B (+89%), 59% data center; $3.0B backlog; FY27 guide $2.4-2.6B.

nodes.name: JST Power Equipment (Jinpan)

nodes.name: Imported distribution transformers (Taiwan, Canada, Mexico, Korea; Eaglerise)

nodes.name: Hammond Power Solutions

nodes.name: Other dry-type makers (Schneider/Square D, Siemens, ABB, ELSCO, Jefferson)

nodes.name: Sunbelt Solomon

nodes.name: Giga Energy

nodes.name: Duke Energy

nodes.name: US residential electricity customers

nodes.name: Anthropic

nodes.name: Household final demand (incl. EVs, heat pumps)

nodes.name: Demand for US-made goods (reshoring)

terms.definition: A large transformer used in transmission and substations to move power between voltage levels, as opposed to the smaller distribution transformers near customers. Where the line falls varies by source; the US tariff schedule splits liquid-filled units at 10 MVA.

A transformer rated above about 100 MVA, used in high-voltage transmission substations and at power plants. Each is custom-engineered, can weigh hundreds of tons, and has the longest lead times in the market. The US has relied on imports for most of its supply.

The transformer at a power plant that raises the generator's output voltage to transmission voltage so the power can travel long distances. Every new gas, hydro or other generating unit needs one, and these units have the longest quoted lead times of any class.

A small transformer near the customer that lowers distribution-line voltage to the level homes and businesses use. Utilities buy them by the thousands as pole-mounts and pad-mounts, and they are far more standardized than power transformers.

A transformer in a utility, industrial or data-center substation that takes power from sub-transmission lines (typically 69-138 kV on this page) down to distribution voltage. The dashboard's preferred entry segment is units of about 10-60 MVA in this class.

Industry shorthand for power transformers between distribution units and large power transformers. 'Small' and 'medium' power together span roughly a few MVA up to about 100 MVA, and makers draw the boundaries differently.

A distribution transformer housed in a locked, ground-level steel cabinet on a concrete pad, used where power lines run underground: subdivisions, commercial sites and data centers. Three-phase pad-mounts are the main transformer type at data-center campuses.
The familiar cylindrical transformer hung on a utility pole, usually single-phase and serving a handful of homes. It is the most standardized and commoditized transformer product.

A factory-built assembly that combines a transformer with its incoming medium-voltage switchgear and outgoing low-voltage distribution equipment in one package, common at industrial sites and data centers.
A transformer cooled by air and insulated with solid materials instead of oil, so it can be installed indoors with lower fire risk. Typical uses are commercial buildings, factories and data centers.
A transformer whose core and windings sit in a tank of insulating oil (or another dielectric fluid) that both insulates and carries away heat. Nearly all utility and power transformers are this type.

A transformer in which part of a single winding is shared between the high- and low-voltage sides. It is smaller and cheaper than a two-winding design and is the usual way to link two transmission networks, such as 765 kV and 345 kV.

The insulated, often porcelain or composite, sleeve that carries a high-voltage conductor through the transformer's grounded metal tank. High-voltage bushings come from few suppliers and are a recognized supply bottleneck.

A mechanism that adjusts a transformer's voltage ratio while it stays energized, by switching between connection points (taps) on a winding. Many power transformers, especially substation units, carry one, and few specialist firms make them.

A device that converts voltage using power electronics (semiconductor switches) rather than a conventional iron core and copper coils. It is smaller and controllable and can supply direct current, but it is costly and unproven at grid scale; start-ups target data centers first.

A transformer and switchgear mounted on a trailer that can be driven to a site and connected quickly, used for emergencies, maintenance outages or temporary service. Rental fleets of these units are part of the aftermarket that private equity is buying.

Switchgear is the assembly of circuit breakers, switches and fuses that controls, protects and isolates equipment; a switchboard is the low-voltage panel that splits power into many circuits inside a building or data center. Both sit next to transformers and are often sold by the same companies.

A large coil connected to a long high-voltage line to absorb excess reactive power and hold voltage steady. Its size is given in MVAr (megavolt-ampere reactive), the unit for reactive power; reactors are built in transformer-type factories and ordered alongside 765 kV transformers.

The core is the stack of thin electrical-steel sheets (laminations) that carries the magnetic field inside a transformer. Makers either cut and stack cores themselves from steel strip or buy finished cores, which are taxed separately from whole transformers.
The coils of insulated copper (or aluminum) wire wrapped around the core; the ratio of turns between windings sets the voltage change. Winding is skilled, largely manual work and a labor bottleneck.

A test bay is the shielded high-voltage laboratory in a transformer factory where finished units are tested before shipment; bigger, higher-voltage units need costlier bays. Type tests are one-time tests on a representative unit proving a design meets standards, which utilities usually require before approving a new supplier.

A factory process that heats the core and coil assembly with solvent vapor under vacuum to drive moisture out of the paper insulation before the unit is filled with oil. The solvent use typically requires an air permit.

Ways of returning a used or failed transformer to service: a rewind replaces the windings while reusing the core and tank, and remanufactured, rebuilt or reconditioned units are repaired and retested for resale. They ship in weeks rather than years, so buyers in a hurry pay prices close to new.

One thousand volts, the unit for line and equipment voltage. In the US, local distribution lines mostly run below about 35 kV and transmission lines from 69 kV up to 765 kV; higher voltage equipment is harder to build and test.

The kVA is the unit for the capacity of smaller transformers: a pole-mount serving a few homes is tens of kVA, a data-center pad-mount a few thousand. Price per kVA ($/kVA) lets buyers compare prices across sizes; bigger units usually cost less per kVA.

An MVA is 1,000 kVA, the usual unit for the capacity of power transformers; a GVA is 1,000 MVA. Substation units are typically tens of MVA, large power transformers are above about 100 MVA, and the biggest exceed 1,000 MVA.

Units of real power: a gigawatt is 1,000 megawatts and a terawatt is 1,000 gigawatts. They measure the size of power plants, data-center loads and grid demand; a large data center campus can draw hundreds of MW.

Power delivered on one alternating-current wave, used by homes and small loads. Very large transmission banks are also often built from three single-phase units because one three-phase unit would be too big to ship.

Power delivered on three overlapping alternating-current waves, the standard for transmission, industry, commercial buildings and data centers. Three-phase transformers are larger and more complex than single-phase ones.
The input (higher-voltage) side of a transformer. A unit with a '69-138 kV primary' takes power in from a sub-transmission line at that voltage.

terms.term: HV / MV / LV (high, medium, low voltage)
terms.definition: Broad voltage classes. LV is below 1 kV (building wiring), MV is roughly 1-35 kV (distribution lines and data-center feeders), and HV covers transmission voltages above that. 'MV/LV' units step medium voltage down to low; 'HV/MV' units step transmission voltage down to medium.
Transmission at roughly 345 kV and above (345, 500 and 765 kV in North America). EHV transformers are the largest and hardest to make, and only a handful of factories can build them.

Strictly, alternating-current transmission at about 800 kV and above. Korean makers and trade press also use the term loosely for their largest high-voltage units, including 345-765 kV transformers sold in the US.
The lightning-surge voltage a transformer's insulation is designed to withstand, stated in kV. A higher BIL means a more robust, harder-to-build unit for a higher-voltage system.

terms.term: GOES (grain-oriented electrical steel) and core steel
terms.definition: Electrical steel is steel made to carry magnetic fields with low energy loss; GOES is the premium grade whose crystal grains are aligned, the critical input for transformer cores. Cleveland-Cliffs is the only US producer and imports face tariffs; 'core steel' on this page covers GOES and finished cores together.

A thin metal ribbon cooled so fast that it never forms crystals, giving lower core losses than GOES. It is used in some high-efficiency distribution transformers, and stricter federal efficiency rules could increase its use.
Refined mineral oil from which transformer insulating oil is made; the fluid fills liquid-filled transformers to insulate and cool them. Its price is a direct input cost.
